newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul financial reform plan still on track - fin min.
newsitem.headline: Seoul financial reform plan still on track - fin min.

text.p: South Korea's finance minister Kang Kyong-shik said on Thursday the government would press ahead with its draft plan on financial reforms despite protests by workers at the central bank and supervisory organisations.

Union workers at the Bank of Korea, the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board have vowed to walk out if the government pushed on with a plan to create a unified supervisory body under the prime minister's control.
"The government will make its best efforts to have the draft plan realised," Kang said in a welcoming speech delivered during an international seminar in Seoul.
The seminar is being sponsored by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform, which since January has been reviewing steps to reform the nation's financial industry.
"The government also plans to soon draw up a draft on other subjects, including the bank ownership issue, after having consultations with related organisations," Kang said.
He was referring to the issue of whether to lift the ceiling of individual ownership in banks now set at four percent.
The commission earlier proposed raising the ceiling to 10 percent under some conditions, but the ministry's draft announced on Monday did not mention the issue.
The ministry's draft has sparked criticism by union workers that the plan would strengthen the government's grip on financial institutions.
In a rare move, senior Bank of Korea officials also demanded that the draft plan be scrapped and called for fresh discussions. The Office of Bank Supervision is now under central bank control.
The ministry's draft also stipulates the Bank of Korea's governor would replace the finance minister as the head of the Monetary Board, the top monetary policy-making body.
Under the new rules, the bank governor would be responsible for setting and meeting annual inflation and other macroeconomic targets.
